did_you_know.text: The incense altar was also called the “golden altar” because it was covered with gold. It was small and designed specifically for burning incense.
The altar was square: one cubit long and wide, and two cubits high. Its four corners had horn-shaped projections, as did other biblical altars.
The rings and poles were used to carry the altar, allowing it to be moved without touching it directly.
The incense was burned twice a day, in the morning and toward evening, at the times when the lamps of the menorah were tended.
The incense altar had a special purpose, so sacrifices, grain offerings, and drink offerings meant for another altar could not be placed on it.
The biblical shekel was not a particular coin but a unit of weight. According to the verse, one shekel consisted of twenty gerah.
Everyone gave the same amount for the half-shekel offering, whether rich or poor. This emphasized the shared participation of the entire people.
The laver was a copper basin placed between the Tent of Meeting and the altar of burnt offering. Its location made it a place of preparation before the priests’ service.
Some of the perfumes in the anointing oil are familiar, such as myrrh and cinnamon, but the exact identity of other ingredients is uncertain.
The anointing oil was prepared as a fragrant mixture by a perfumer, not as ordinary oil. Its careful preparation emphasized its special status.
The Hebrew verb for anointing, mashach, is related to the word mashiach, meaning someone anointed for a special role. Here, anointing marked the priestly role.
The anointing oil was not meant for personal or everyday use. The prohibition teaches that a sacred object does not become ordinary simply because a similar product can be made.
The incense also lists fragrant substances whose exact identities are debated. Scholars and commentators do not agree precisely on the meanings of nataf, shechelet, and chelbenah.
